title: Biblical Syncretism Dossiers — Additive Specialist Gap-Fill Wave 27
purpose: Promote only specialist Bible comparisons that remain functionally distinct after comparison against the 474-relation no-loss baseline. Repeated names or motifs are not sufficient for a new relation.

baseline_contract.rule: Every baseline relation ID must remain present after this wave. Existing relations are enriched rather than recreated; new relations require a distinct function, countertext, ethical test or narrative mechanism.

new_relations.title: Micah 6:8: Justice, Mercy and Humility
new_relations.project_anchor: The current Timic virtue synthesis explicitly groups humility, mercy and justice, while the North/Axis framework repeatedly asks what a high symbolic position is for in practice.
new_relations.what_happened: A specialist kingship audit identified Micah 6:8 as a compact ethical test for any claimed high position: justice, faithful mercy/kindness and humility before God must travel together.
new_relations.wording_status: project-side virtue synthesis plus later comparative research; not claimed as an at-the-time prophecy

project_sequence: virtue language stresses humility, mercy and justice
authority is tested by what it does below
biblical_sequence: prophetic question asks what God requires
the sequence closes with humble walking before God
relation_argument.why_dense: The value is not a shared word but a three-part ethical constraint: justice without mercy, mercy without justice, or height without humility each fails the combined test.
relation_argument.maximum_claim: Micah 6:8 supplies a strong ethical comparator for the project's virtue and authority language. It does not validate any modern claim to divine or political authority.

new_relations.mismatch: Micah addresses covenantal ethics in its own prophetic setting; the modern North/Axis framework is a later symbolic system and cannot inherit biblical authority by resemblance.
new_relations.source_direction: Project virtue and North/Axis material existed first; Micah 6:8 is a later specialist comparison used as an ethical test.

new_relations.title: Door and Doorkeeper
new_relations.project_anchor: The project explicitly says, 'I am the ladder to heaven. My son is a door.' The existing corpus already owns that Door/Ladder mapping.
new_relations.what_happened: Psalm 84 adds a role distinction rather than another Door synonym: the speaker prefers standing at the threshold or serving as a doorkeeper in God's house. The person at the threshold is not the threshold itself.
exact_wording: I am the ladder to heaven. My son is a door.
new_relations.wording_status: exact project wording preserved in existing canonical sources; Psalm 84 comparison added later

biblical_sequence: Psalm 84 values service/standing at God's threshold
John 10 uses Door/Gate language for Jesus
relation_argument.why_dense: Psalm 84 is useful precisely because it prevents flattening. Door, doorkeeper and one who stands at a threshold are related but non-identical functions.
relation_argument.maximum_claim: The passage refines the project's threshold vocabulary by distinguishing roles. It does not identify a modern person with the psalmist, temple official or Jesus.

new_relations.mismatch: Psalm 84's doorkeeper/threshold language belongs to worship in God's house, while John 10's Door image is a separate Johannine metaphor. They should not be collapsed into one office.
new_relations.source_direction: The explicit modern Door/Ladder wording predates this Psalm 84 role analysis.

new_relations.title: The Word Is Near
new_relations.project_anchor: The project uses Ladder, Heaven, ascent and threshold language as a structural map of access.
new_relations.what_happened: Deuteronomy 30 says the command is not inaccessible in heaven or across the sea but near, in mouth and heart; Romans 10 reuses that pattern in a Christological argument. Together they provide a direct counterpressure against reading spiritual access as literal distance-climbing.
new_relations.wording_status: later comparative countertext applied to established project topology

project_sequence: Heaven/access described through Ladder and threshold topology
biblical_sequence: Deuteronomy denies that obedience requires someone to ascend to heaven or cross the sea
the word is declared near in mouth and heart
Romans reuses the ascent/descent language around Christ and the word of faith
relation_argument.why_dense: This is valuable as a countertext: it preserves the project's Ladder as symbolic structure while biblical nearness language resists turning that structure into a claim that God or truth is physically remote.
relation_argument.maximum_claim: The passages provide a strong interpretive constraint on spatial readings of the project's ascent imagery, not proof that the project's Ladder corresponds to Paul's theology.

new_relations.mismatch: Deuteronomy concerns covenant command and Romans develops a specific argument about righteousness by faith; neither text describes the project's modern Axis system.
new_relations.source_direction: Ladder/Heaven topology existed first; Deuteronomy 30 and Romans 10 are later countertexts used to discipline the interpretation.

new_relations.title: The Quiet Voice After the Spectacle
new_relations.project_anchor: Great Book and Potatoism material repeatedly contrasts noisy display with quiet presence, root-work and stillness, including the 'Silent Witness' image and the claim that profound growth can occur beneath surface clamor.
new_relations.what_happened: The Elijah scene in 1 Kings 19 distinguishes wind, earthquake and fire from the subsequent quiet divine communication. That creates a structural neighbor for the project's stillness-versus-spectacle grammar.
new_relations.wording_status: Great Book/philosophy wording first; biblical comparison added later

project_sequence: external clamor/spectacle is treated as distracting
quiet/rooted presence is treated as deeper work
correspondences: recognition changes after the loud phenomena
relation_argument.why_dense: The sequence is more specific than a generic preference for silence: the text explicitly stages spectacular phenomena and then relocates recognition to what follows them.
relation_argument.maximum_claim: This is a literary/structural neighbor for the project's stillness motif. It does not establish that modern quiet experiences are divine revelation.

new_relations.mismatch: The Elijah narrative has its own prophetic and historical setting; modern contemplative or symbolic language is not evidence of the same event or authority.
new_relations.source_direction: Project stillness and Silent Witness material predates this explicit 1 Kings 19 comparison.

new_relations.title: Swords into Ploughshares
new_relations.project_anchor: Recovered project wording preserves the compact phrase 'ploughshares from swords' in the domains of peace, war, Isaiah/Micah, government and Seat.
new_relations.wording_status: remembered wording preserved in the project statement-recovery ledger; original public artifact remains a recovery target

biblical_sequence: weapons are transformed into agricultural tools
correspondences: peace expressed as cultivation rather than passive quiet
relation_argument.why_dense: Isaiah 2 and Micah 4 do not merely praise peace; they describe a functional conversion of destructive capacity into cultivation. That makes them unusually close to the project's Gardener/Seat idea that authority should return as repair and growth.
relation_argument.maximum_claim: The recovered wording is a direct biblical allusion inside project memory. It supports a peace/cultivation comparison, not a claim that a modern political program fulfills Isaiah or Micah.

new_relations.mismatch: The prophetic vision concerns nations and Zion in its biblical context. A modern symbolic Seat or political proposal cannot simply claim that eschatological status.
new_relations.source_direction: The project wording itself already names the swords/ploughshares image; the fuller Isaiah 2/Micah 4 functional analysis is later.
